title: Harness Platform Overview
content: Harness is a software delivery platform that unifies continuous integration, continuous delivery, feature management, security testing, cloud cost management, service reliability, chaos engineering, and infrastructure-as-code management behind a single control plane. The product family is organized as a set of first-party modules that share an identity, RBAC, audit log, and secrets manager. The platform is delivered as a managed SaaS and as a self-hosted (Harness Self-Managed Enterprise Edition) deployment for regulated environments. First-class integrations exist for Kubernetes, AWS, GCP, Azure, and the major artifact repositories.

title: CI Pipelines Overview
content: A Harness CI pipeline is a YAML-defined graph of stages executed in order, in parallel, or via fan-out/fan-in. Each pipeline is owned by an organization, a project, and optionally an account. Pipelines run on Harness-managed build infrastructure (Harness Cloud) or on self-hosted runners (Kubernetes, VMs, or Docker). The model deliberately separates the pipeline definition (checked into the repo) from the run-time concerns (secrets, connectors, service accounts), so a single pipeline can promote across dev, staging, and prod without duplicating the YAML. Inputs can be supplied via triggers, runtime inputs, or fixed values.

title: Pipeline Stages
content: A stage is the atomic unit of execution in Harness. A CI stage typically contains steps such as BuildAndPushDockerRegistry, CacheIntelligence, RunTests, GitClone, Plugin, Background, and more. CD stages include Deploy, Apply, Rollback, Approval, and Custom. Each stage has its own failure strategy (the default is to fail the pipeline) and can declare its own service identity, infrastructure, and environment. Stages can be marked as parallel or sequential, and step groups can be parallelized within a stage.

title: Pipeline Execution Semantics
content: A Harness pipeline executes top-to-bottom respecting dependency edges. A stage can declare itself parallel, which means it runs concurrently with siblings under the same parallel group. A step group within a stage can also be parallel. Matrix strategies (loops over a list of inputs) multiply the stage across combinations, and conditional execution uses runtime expressions ("<+input>" or expressions like "<+pipeline.variables.env> == 'prod'"). Failure strategies include Ignore, Abort, MarkAsSuccess, Retry, and Rollback.

title: Continuous Delivery Overview
content: Harness CD is a GitOps-aware deployment orchestrator. It models a Service (the thing being deployed), an Environment (where it runs), and an Infrastructure Definition (the actual cluster or VM). A pipeline can deploy the same Service to many Environments in sequence with stage-level gates between them. The platform integrates with Helm, Kustomize, native Kubernetes manifests, Terraform, and most major IaaS providers. Canary, blue/green, and rolling deployments are first-class. Continuous Verification (CV) lets Harness observe a canary using Datadog, Splunk, Dynatrace, Prometheus, or AppD, and automatically promote or rollback based on SLOs.

title: Deployment Strategies
content: Harness CD supports rolling, canary, blue/green, and recreate strategies. Rolling replaces pods in batches, controlled by maxUnavailable and maxSurge. Canary splits traffic by a percentage and advances through stages (e.g., 10% → 25% → 50% → 100%) with optional manual or automatic promotion. Blue/Green provisions a parallel stack and flips the service routing atomically. Recreate is the simplest: stop the old, start the new. The choice is set on the Kubernetes or Helm service definition, and the pipeline stage references that definition.

title: GitOps with Harness
content: Harness GitOps uses Argo CD as the reconciliation engine under the hood. A GitOps Application defines the source (a Git repo) and the destination (a cluster + namespace). Harness treats the cluster as the source of truth, drift detection runs on a schedule, and self-heal can revert cluster changes back to the Git state. The recommended pattern is to keep application manifests in a separate repo from the pipeline code. Harness ships ApplicationSet and Sync Wave support so multi-cluster fan-out and ordered rollouts are declarative.

title: Feature Flags Overview
content: Harness Feature Management is a feature-flag and experimentation service. Flags are organized by environment; a flag can have multiple variations (treatments) and targeting rules. SDKs exist for web, mobile, and server. The platform supports percentage rollouts, user/segment targeting, and kill switches. Experiment metrics can be connected to a metrics provider (Datadog, New Relic, Snowflake) to compute statistical significance. The flag pipeline is the same pattern as CD: a change in a flag's targeting rules is a deployable artifact.

title: A/B Testing and Experimentation
content: An experiment in Harness is a feature flag with a metric attribution. When a user is bucketed into a treatment, the SDK fires an impression event tagged with the experiment id. The metrics service joins these impressions with downstream conversion data (revenue, signups, retention) and computes lift with confidence intervals. The minimum sample size and runtime are configurable per experiment. Results are exposed in a dashboard and via API, and the winning variation can be promoted to 100% with a single click.

title: Security Testing Orchestration (STO)
content: STO integrates scanners (SAST, DAST, SCA, container, IaC, secrets) into Harness pipelines. A Security Tests stage declares a target (image, repo, instance), a scanner (Snyk, Checkmarx, Veracode, OWASP ZAP, Trivy, Aqua, Prisma Cloud, etc.), and a severity threshold. The stage fails the pipeline if vulnerabilities above the threshold are detected. Scans can be reused across pipelines via shared security test steps, and results are aggregated in the STO dashboard with deduplication and exemption workflows.

title: SAST, DAST, and SCA
content: SAST (static analysis) scans source code without executing it. DAST (dynamic analysis) exercises a running instance with crafted inputs. SCA (software composition analysis) inventories third-party dependencies and flags known CVEs. Harness STO supports each category through dedicated scanner integrations. The key practical difference: SAST and SCA run early in the pipeline (after checkout), DAST runs against a deployed environment later (after a stage deploy). Severity thresholds are usually tuned by team, not by pipeline.

title: Cloud Cost Management (CCM)
content: CCM is Harness's FinOps module. It connects to AWS, GCP, and Azure via read-only roles, ingests billing and utilization data, and groups it by Harness perspectives (services, environments, teams, clusters). It detects idle resources, RI/SP coverage gaps, and cost anomalies. Budgets can be set on a perspective and a notification fires when burn rate exceeds the threshold. CCM also surfaces recommendations for rightsizing, idle cleanup, and commitment discount purchases, with one-click integrations into Jira or ServiceNow for ticketing.

title: Cost Anomaly Detection
content: Anomaly detection in CCM uses a per-perspective baseline (14-day rolling median) and a configurable sensitivity (1.0–3.0 standard deviations). When actual spend exceeds the threshold, an alert is generated and routed by perspective owner. Anomalies are tagged by category: spend spike, new resource, data transfer, commitment expiration. The detail page shows top contributors, a day-by-day breakdown, and the option to dismiss, suppress for a window, or open a ticket. The model retrains daily and the baseline is updated incrementally.

title: Service Reliability Management (SRM)
content: SRM is Harness's SLO and error-tracking module. An SLO is a Service Level Objective defined over an SLI (e.g., 99.9% of requests return < 500ms over 30 days). The error budget is consumed when the SLI is violated. SRM uses burn-rate windows (1h, 6h, 24h, 3d) to detect fast and slow budget consumption. When the budget is at risk, alerts fire to PagerDuty, Slack, or email. SLO health can be a CD promotion gate: a canary cannot be promoted to 100% if the error budget is already exhausted.

title: Designing SLIs
content: An SLI is a ratio of good events to total events. The most useful SLIs are user-facing: successful HTTP requests (2xx/3xx vs. all), latency below a threshold, or workflow completion events. Avoid vanity SLIs (CPU, memory) — they are not user-perceived. A good rule: each SLO has 1–3 SLIs, and each SLI is something you can actually graph in your observability tool. The platform accepts SLI data from Datadog, Splunk, Dynatrace, New Relic, Prometheus, and a generic OTel endpoint.

title: Chaos Engineering
content: Harness Chaos (formerly LitmusChaos, which Harness acquired) is a controlled-failure platform. Chaos Experiments are declarative and run probes (steady-state hypotheses) before, during, and after faults. Fault types include pod kill, network latency, CPU stress, disk fill, DNS spoof, AZ failure simulation, and many more. Experiments are version-controlled in Git and run on a schedule or as part of a CD pipeline stage. The recommended pattern: start in staging, observe the steady state survive, then promote the experiment to prod on a canary cohort.

title: Internal Developer Portal (IDP)
content: The IDP is a self-service catalog for engineering teams. It exposes Services, Environments, APIs, Pipelines, and Onboarding Workflows as a Software Catalog (inspired by Backstage). Developers can request a new service, deploy a sandbox, and onboard a new repo from a single page. The catalog is populated automatically from Kubernetes, GitHub, and Harness itself. Scorecards surface team-level health (SLO coverage, test coverage, ownership). The IDP is the recommended landing page for new engineers.

title: Infrastructure as Code Management (IaCM)
content: IaCM is Harness's managed Terraform and OpenTofu orchestrator. It runs `terraform plan` and `terraform apply` with state stored in Harness, integrates with VCS for module versioning, and enforces OPA policies on every plan. Drift detection runs against managed workspaces and produces a PR with a remediation. IaCM stages are first-class in CD pipelines — a service deploy can be preceded by an IaCM apply of its networking, with rollbacks on both sides linked.

title: Software Supply Chain Assurance (SSCA)
content: SSCA generates and verifies SLSA-compliant build provenance. The pipeline captures the build environment, source identity, and dependency graph at build time, signs the artifact (Cosign / Sigstore), and writes a verifiable provenance attestation. Consumers can verify that an artifact was built from a specific commit using a verified builder. SSCA integrates with STO so that vulnerable dependencies block the artifact from being promoted. This is the recommended path for orgs subject to executive order 14028 or similar supply chain mandates.

title: Harness Code Repository
content: Harness Code is a managed Git service based on Gitea. It provides pull requests, branch policies, code search, and webhooks. The unique value versus GitHub or GitLab is the tight integration with Harness pipelines: a PR event is a first-class pipeline trigger and the pipeline status posts back to the PR. CODEOWNERS and required-status-checks work the same as on GitHub. For orgs already on GitHub, the recommendation is usually to keep using GitHub and only adopt Harness Code for new orgs or air-gapped deployments.

title: Kubernetes Integration
content: The Harness Kubernetes connector targets a cluster via a service account token or a Kubernetes cloud provider. The connector caches cluster facts (namespaces, deployments) to speed up manifest resolution. Manifests can be sourced as a remote Git repo, a Harness File Store entry, or a Harness Code repo. The service definition picks the manifest type: Native Kubernetes, Helm, Kustomize, or OpenShift Template. Substitution is enabled by default, and values can come from a values YAML, runtime inputs, or Harness variables.

title: AWS Deployments
content: Harness deploys to ECS, EKS, Lambda, EC2, and S3 via the AWS Cloud Provider connector. ECS deployments support rolling, canary, and blue/green with ALB target group manipulation. Lambda deployments can use the SAM/Serverless Framework integration or the native AWS Lambda step. EC2 deployments use the AMI-as-blueprint or the Amazon ECS Anywhere step. S3 deployments are typically used for static sites; the step syncs a build artifact to a bucket and invalidates CloudFront.

title: GCP Deployments
content: Harness supports GKE, Cloud Run, Cloud Functions, App Engine, and Compute Engine. The GCP Cloud Provider connector uses a service account JSON key. Cloud Run is the recommended target for stateless HTTP services; Harness handles revision tagging and traffic splitting. GKE mirrors the EKS support for canary, blue/green, and rolling. For Cloud SQL migrations, the recommended pattern is a manual approval step plus a SQL change window recorded in a Pipeline Variable.

title: Azure Deployments
content: Harness supports AKS, Azure Web Apps, Azure Functions, and Azure VMSS. The Azure Cloud Provider connector uses a service principal or a workload identity federation. AKS has the same canary/blue/green/rolling story as EKS and GKE. Web Apps deployments use zip deploy and slot swap for blue/green. For VMSS, Harness uses the Azure VMSS custom script extension; rolling is the only strategy.

title: GitHub Integration
content: The GitHub connector authenticates via a personal access token, a GitHub App installation, or a fine-grained token. Triggers can fire on Pull Request, Push, Tag, or Schedule. The PR trigger is most common — it produces a Pull Request pipeline that runs in the context of the PR head, comments back with the status check, and is automatically deleted on PR close. Status checks support required checks for branch protection. Webhooks and the Checks API are both supported.

title: Secrets Management
content: Harness has a built-in secret manager and integrates with HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, and CyberArk. The secret reference syntax is `<+secrets.getValue("my_secret")>`. Secrets are resolved at runtime in the build environment, never written to logs, and masked in the UI. The recommended pattern: use a different secret per environment (dev/staging/prod) and restrict read access via Harness RBAC to the role that needs it.

title: Pipeline as Code
content: Harness pipelines can be defined in the UI or as YAML checked into the repo. The YAML lives under `.harness/` at the repo root. The remote pipeline-as-code flow: the pipeline is committed to a branch, Harness validates the YAML on push, and on merge to main the pipeline is synced. The advantage over UI-only is that changes go through the standard PR review, and the pipeline evolves with the service. The YAML is intentionally not a full superset of the UI model — some advanced features (e.g., parallel groups) are UI-only at the time of writing.

title: Troubleshooting: Init Step Failures
content: If a Harness CI step fails at the Initialize phase, the most common causes are: (1) the connector has insufficient IAM permissions to fetch secrets or clone the repo, (2) the build infrastructure (CI runner) cannot reach the required network endpoints (registry, artifact store), (3) the service account used by the connector has been rotated or deleted. The first debugging step is to enable the Pipeline Execution URL and inspect the step logs; the second is to test the connector with a minimal pipeline. The Init step does not show the user code yet, so failures here are always environment, not code.

title: Troubleshooting: OOM During Build
content: Out-of-memory kills during the Build step usually mean the build tool (Maven, Gradle, Node, Go) is using more heap than the runner provides. On Harness Cloud runners, the default is 4GB. Increase it on the Build stage under Resource Limits. The other common cause is parallel test execution: a test runner with N parallel workers will roughly multiply memory use by N/2. Cap parallelism with `-T 1` (Make), `--max-workers=1` (Node), or `-parallel 1` (Go). Long-term, push the test suite onto a separate Run Tests stage with a larger resource class.

title: Pricing & Licensing
content: Harness sells primarily by active committers and by module. The Team tier is per-developer-seat and includes Pipelines, CD, Feature Flags, and IDP at a basic level. The Enterprise tier adds advanced features: STO, CCM, Chaos, SSCA, IaCM, advanced RBAC, audit log streaming, and self-managed deployment. Some modules (CCM, CCM anomaly detection, Chaos enterprise features) are also billed by cloud spend under management. Most enterprise contracts include SSO/SAML, dedicated support, and an SLA. Pricing is not published in detail; it requires a sales engagement.

title: Canary Deployment Percentages
content: Harness CD expresses a canary as a series of steps with increasing traffic percentages. The recommended starter sequence is 10% → 25% → 50% → 100%, with an approval gate between each. Each step can have its own soak time (e.g., 5 min at 10%, 15 min at 25%) and a Continuous Verification check that compares the canary error rate against the baseline. If CV flags a regression, the stage aborts and the rollback step runs. For low-risk services the 10% step can be skipped; for high-risk services (financial transactions, medical) the sequence can extend to 1% → 5% → 10% → 25% → 50% → 100%.

title: RBAC and Roles
content: Harness RBAC operates on three axes: scope (account, org, project), resource (pipeline, service, environment, secret, etc.), and action (view, edit, delete, deploy, manage). Predefined roles (Project Admin, Project Developer, Project Viewer) cover 90% of needs. Custom roles can be defined for fine-grained access (e.g., a Release Manager who can deploy but cannot edit pipelines). User groups map to an identity provider (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace) and can be granted one or more roles. Service accounts are non-human accounts used by triggers and external systems.

title: Triggers
content: A trigger is the thing that starts a pipeline. Triggers can be webhook-based (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Harness Code), scheduled (cron), or manual. A Webhook trigger can filter on branch, event type (PR opened, push, tag), file path (e.g., only fire when `infra/**` changes), and payload content. Scheduled triggers are useful for nightly builds, weekly cost reports, or periodic chaos experiments. Triggers can also pass conditions (expressions) to decide whether to actually run.

title: Approvals
content: An Approval stage pauses the pipeline and waits for a human or an automated gate to sign off. The human approval lists specific users, user groups, or roles; multiple approvers can be required (any of, all of, or N of M). The automated approval can be an HTTP call to an external system (ServiceNow, Jira) or an expression on pipeline variables. Approval windows can have a timeout that triggers a failure strategy (Abort, Ignore, Rollback).

title: Audit Log
content: Every action in Harness is logged with who did it, when, from where, and what changed. The audit log is searchable in the UI, exportable via API, and streamable to a SIEM (Splunk, Sumo, Datadog, New Relic, generic webhook) for retention beyond the 30-day default. Common audit events: pipeline created, pipeline edited, pipeline executed, secret accessed, role granted, deploy triggered. Audit logs are append-only and immutable. Enterprise tier customers can also forward to a custom S3/GCS bucket.
